post.caption: Electrum shares its name with electricity. The Greek word for amber also named a gold and silver alloy. In 1600, William Gilbert coined electricus, meaning like amber. Pliny wrote that gold with a fifth silver was called electrum. In the 6th century BC, goldsmiths at Sardis refined it with salt. The salt changed the silver so the clay could soak it up. In 1968, diggers spotted greenish rings on a clay floor at Sardis. The gold they recovered was only tiny specks like pinheads. Egyptians coated obelisk tops in electrum so they flashed in the sun. The Greeks called electrum white gold.
